card_roles.Hapatra, Vizier of Poisons: Cast her turn two and forget the combat trigger — an unevasive 2/2 rarely connects, and that half is a bonus. Build around the other half: one 1/1 deathtouch Snake for every placement event where you put -1/-1 counters on a creature.
card_roles.Yawgmoth, Thran Physician: Your default tutor target. Of the eight sacrifice outlets here that cost no mana he is the only one that also places a counter, so he is outlet, Snake factory and draw engine on one body. Have a second creature before you start: the counter needs a target that is not the thing you just ate.
card_roles.Mikaeus, the Unhallowed: Six mana, and he pays for it only with a partner — Devoted Druid or Walking Ballista plus an outlet. Know two things before you cast him: he does nothing for Hapatra or Yawgmoth, who are both Human, and he makes your Snakes 2/2, which nothing here has settled the token loops' opinion of.
card_roles.Devoted Druid: A mana dork whose untap ability pays a -1/-1 counter — a free repeatable counter source hiding in the ramp slot. With Mikaeus out it resets itself forever; without him, run it down for two green, two Snakes and a body in the graveyard whenever the turn needs it.
card_roles.Walking Ballista: Removal you can hold at any size, and the cleanest verified kill in the deck when Mikaeus and any free outlet join it. Cast it for X=1 early if it buys a body; save it if the table is presenting nothing worth shooting.
card_roles.Blowfly Infestation: Every creature that dies with a -1/-1 counter puts another counter on something — that is a repeatable source, and repeatable sources are the scarce class. Play it for exactly that. The two-card kill it is famous for is unresolved here; do not build a turn around it.
card_roles.Nest of Scarabs: The best exchange rate you own: the -1/-1 counters you place come back as that many 1/1 Insects, so a two-counter placement is two bodies. Watch the templating — it pays only when you are the one placing them.
card_roles.Flourishing Defenses: Five mana, and it triggers on any -1/-1 counter placed on any creature by anyone. Slower than Nest of Scarabs and broader; take it when the table is also spraying counters, and do not lead your curve with it.
card_roles.Obelisk Spider: The converter worth tutoring for. It drains each opponent on counter placement rather than on death, so it prices any loop several times faster than a dies-trigger does — and reach plus a combat-damage counter makes it a real blocker while you set up.
card_roles.Zulaport Cutthroat: Each opponent loses one for every creature you control that dies. That is your table clock; deploy it the turn before you go off, not four turns early where it invites removal.
card_roles.Bastion of Remembrance: The same drain in enchantment form, which means a wrath cannot answer it, and it brings its own Soldier along. Against a table with sweepers, lead with this converter over the creatures.
card_roles.Blood Artist: One target player per death, not each — a wrath tax and a value engine, never your clock. Point the drains at whoever is closest to dead, and take the incidental life.
card_roles.Skullclamp: Equip a 1/1 Snake, watch it die, draw two for one mana. Do it every turn you have spare mana and a spare body; this is the card that turns your tokens into a deck.
card_roles.Grim Haruspex: Draws off your nontoken deaths only, so he pays for the real creatures — Snakes and Insects do nothing for him. Three mana, and he replaces himself the moment a wrath lands.
card_roles.Morbid Opportunist: Once a turn, any creature dying anywhere hands you a card. That means he draws on every opponent's turn too — leave him back and let three other players work for you.
card_roles.Deadly Dispute: Two cards and a Treasure at instant speed for a body that was already fodder. Fire it in response to removal on the creature you were about to sacrifice anyway.
card_roles.Village Rites: One black, two cards, one dead Snake. The cheapest way to turn a wrath or a targeted kill into card advantage — hold it for that turn rather than spending it on curve.
card_roles.Night's Whisper: Two cards for two mana and two life. Unremarkable, and exactly what a hand with an engine and no fuel needs on turn two.
card_roles.The One Ring: The single biggest draw turn you own, plus a turn of protection from everything when you cast it. Take it when you want the cards; the burden counters compound, so plan the turn you cash it and the turn you stop.
card_roles.Demonic Tutor: Two mana, any card, no strings. Fetch a repeatable counter source first and a converter second — that ordering is the whole tutor policy of this deck.
card_roles.Grim Tutor: Demonic Tutor for a mana and three life more. Your life total is a resource here anyway; spend it and get the source.
card_roles.Diabolic Intent: Any card to hand, and the sacrifice is nearly free — the body was fodder, and its death is a trigger for half your board. Sequence it after you have a Snake to spare.
card_roles.Vampiric Tutor: Instant speed, top of library, two life. Use it on an opponent's end step so the card you fetch arrives with a full turn of mana behind it.
card_roles.Imperial Seal: The sorcery-speed version, and it costs one black. Fire it on a turn you were not going to use all your mana, because the card does not arrive until your next draw.
card_roles.Worldly Tutor: Instant speed for a creature, on top. Grab Yawgmoth or Obelisk Spider at end of turn and untap into it.
card_roles.Survival of the Fittest: Repeatable creature tutoring for one green, discarding a creature you would rather have in the graveyard anyway with Phyrexian Reclamation out. Left alone it finds every creature in your deck.
card_roles.Green Sun's Zenith: Puts a green creature straight onto the battlefield, which beats drawing one. X=2 is Devoted Druid; X=0 or 1 is a dork on the turn you need the mana more.
card_roles.Ashnod's Altar: A free outlet that turns every spare body into two colourless mana, which is genuine acceleration in a deck that makes bodies for nothing. Its famous Mikaeus pairing is refuted — use it as a mana engine and a sacrifice engine, not a combo piece.
card_roles.Phyrexian Altar: The coloured version: any body, any colour, no mana in the cost. The colour matters more than you think when your black pips run to triple.
card_roles.Carrion Feeder: One mana, sacrifices at will, and it grows. Just know that it puts +1/+1 counters on itself, which is precisely the wrong direction under Mikaeus.
card_roles.Viscera Seer: A one-mana free outlet that smooths your draws. Sacrifice in response to removal every single time; the scry is small, and free is free.
card_roles.Blasting Station: Untaps whenever a creature enters, so a stream of tokens becomes repeatable damage with no drain payoff needed at all. This is your out when the table has hosed lifeloss.
card_roles.Yahenni, Undying Partisan: A free outlet with haste that shrugs off wraths by going indestructible. Sacrifice a Snake in response to the sweeper and keep your three-drop.
card_roles.Fume Spitter: One mana, sacrifices itself, places a counter. That is a Snake, a trigger and a dead one-toughness creature for the cheapest price in the deck — do not hold it hoping for a better target.
card_roles.Serrated Arrows: Three counters, three activations, three Snakes, spread over three turns. Slow and repeatable, which is exactly the class this deck is short of.
card_roles.Contagion Clasp: A counter on arrival, then proliferate for four whenever you have nothing better. Late, it turns one counter on an opponent's creature into a kill and a Snake at the same time.
card_roles.Grim Affliction: A counter plus proliferate at instant speed. Best used when two or more of your counters are already sitting on the board waiting to be finished.
card_roles.Crumbling Ashes: Repeating unconditional removal in a deck that puts counters on things every turn. Read the trigger before you place counters on your own creatures — it destroys target creature with a counter, and it fires whether you like the target or not.
card_roles.Black Sun's Zenith: Not a reset — a rebuild. X counters on each creature leaves your counter payoffs a board to work with and hands Necroskitter every opposing creature that dies with a counter on it. Cast it for the number that kills their side and leaves yours breathing.
card_roles.Toxic Deluge: Minus X to everything for X life, and it places no counters — no Snakes, no Insects, no Necroskitter returns. Treat it as the panic button it is, and reach for Black Sun's Zenith first whenever you have the mana.
card_roles.Necroskitter: Every creature an opponent controls that dies with a -1/-1 counter comes back under your control. Against a creature table, place counters on their board rather than yours and let the sweeper do the rest.
card_roles.Host of the Hereafter: A four-mana body that arrives with two +1/+1 counters and moves counters off your dying creatures onto a survivor. The loop it is listed for is unverified; play it as a value body that keeps your counters on the board.
card_roles.Ivy Lane Denizen: Your Snakes are green, so every one of them puts a +1/+1 counter on a creature of your choice. Use that to save a creature from your own -1/-1 counters, and treat the Scurry Oak line as unresolved rather than as a plan.
card_roles.Scurry Oak: Evolves, and makes a Squirrel every time it gains a +1/+1 counter. A fine body that makes bodies; the combo it is named for has not been settled here.
card_roles.Sephiroth, Fabled SOLDIER // Sephiroth,: Sacrifices a creature and draws when it enters or attacks, and drains an opponent on every other creature's death. Four drain resolutions in one turn flips it — count them on the turn you go wide, because that transformation is free value you can actually plan for.
card_roles.Pitiless Plunderer: Every other creature you control that dies leaves a Treasure, tokens included. That is what pays for the expensive half of your turn after a sweeper resolves.
card_roles.Bitterblossom: A free flying body every upkeep for one life. Fodder, chump blocker, Skullclamp target, and the reason you survive a wrath — deploy it turn two and never think about it again.
card_roles.Eternal Witness: Rebuys the tutor, the sweeper or the engine piece that got answered, on a body that is itself fodder. Hold it until they have actually spent the removal.
card_roles.Phyrexian Reclamation: One black up front, then two life and two mana buys any creature back, forever. This is the card that makes a wrath a delay instead of a defeat.
card_roles.Heroic Intervention: Hold it for the turn you go, not the turn you feel sad. It answers targeted removal and destruction across your whole board for two mana.
card_roles.Lightning Greaves: Free equip, haste and shroud. It gets your commander or Yawgmoth online the turn they land — but shroud means Hapatra and Yawgmoth can no longer target the creature wearing them, so move it before you start placing counters.
card_roles.Swiftfoot Boots: Hexproof and haste for one to equip, and the hexproof only stops opponents, so you can still target your own creature. Slower than the Greaves and strictly friendlier to your engine.
card_roles.Orcish Bowmasters: Flash, a body, a ping and an Orc, and it punishes every extra card three opponents draw. Hold it up on their turn rather than casting it on yours.
card_roles.Birds of Paradise: Turn-one acceleration that fixes both colours, blocks fliers, and later doubles as fodder and a Skullclamp target. Lead with it over the Elves when the hand needs black on turn two.
card_roles.Llanowar Elves: Green on turn one, which is a two-mana commander on turn one when a black source comes with it. Spend it as fodder without a second thought once the mana is no longer the problem.
card_roles.Elvish Mystic: The same card again, and the redundancy is the point — you want the turn-one dork more often than you want any particular one.
card_roles.Dark Ritual: Three black off one, which is Hapatra on turn one or Yawgmoth on turn two. Do not hold it for a hypothetical bigger turn; the deck's biggest turns cost four.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colourless on turn one, and it makes none of your coloured mana. Cast it first and let the lands handle the pips.
card_roles.Mana Vault: Three mana on the turn you need four, at the price of a damage a turn while it sits tapped. Untap it when the game is long, not out of habit.
card_roles.Grim Monolith: Three colourless from a two-drop. Perfect on turn two into a four-drop, awkward afterwards — spend it early rather than saving it.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Two mana, and it makes the colour you actually need every single time. Unglamorous, never dead.
card_roles.Lotus Petal: One mana of any colour, once, for free. Save it for the turn it makes a real difference, and remember it is also an artifact for Deadly Dispute.
card_roles.Chrome Mox: Free acceleration that exiles a coloured card from your hand. In a singleton deck that is a real cost — imprint the redundant dork, never the tutor.
card_roles.Mox Diamond: Free acceleration that eats a land. Keep it only in hands with enough lands to spare one, and remember what the land-drop rate does to you later in the game.
card_roles.Fixing lands: Bayou, Command Tower, City of Brass, Mana Confluence, Exotic Orchard, Spire of Industry, Conduit Pylons, Gond Gate, Hidden Grotto, Darkbore Pathway, Wastewood Verge, The Grey Havens, Tarnished Citadel, Forbidden Orchard and Gemstone Caverns, plus seven Swamps and seven Forests. None of them enters tapped, so lead with the painless ones early and pay the life when you need the colour.
card_roles.Utility lands: Grim Backwoods, Svogthos, Lazotep Quarry, Opal Palace, Talon Gates of Madara, The Mycosynth Gardens and Abstergo Entertainment do a second job — a sacrifice outlet, a creature land, a reanimation, extra counters on a recast commander, a phase-out, an artifact copy and the deck's only graveyard answer. Play them on the turns your colours are already covered.

combo_lines.001:
The clause that decides this case sits inside undying itself: return it "if it had no +1/+1 counters on it" (CR 702.93a). Undying hands the creature back wearing exactly such a counter. The off-switch is inside the ability.

The claim was that Hapatra strips it. Counter annihilation is real and automatic — a permanent holding one of each loses both as a state-based action (CR 704.5q) — but her placement is a combat-damage trigger, not an at-will one. She cannot be interleaved between sacrifices. Holding: the claim fails as written.

Two exhibits follow it down. A sacrificed Snake token ceases to exist in the state-based check that precedes its own undying trigger reaching the stack (CR 704.5d), so the token version produces zero iterations, not infinite ones. And six listed pairings — Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Yahenni, Blasting Station — buy exactly one extra death apiece before the intervening "if" turns false.

What the record does support: Mikaeus with Devoted Druid, unbounded in deaths, counters and Snakes but not in mana, because the returned Druid is a new object barred from tapping (CR 302.6). Mikaeus with Walking Ballista, genuinely unbounded and a three-card assembly, since layer 7c makes a counterless Ballista a 1/1 rather than a 0/0 (CR 613.4c). Yawgmoth, looping for real and bounded by the library his own mandatory draw empties.

The sheet claims nineteen two-card infinites. This record verifies one, refutes six, and on the remainder it is silent.

cover.identity: You are playing a converter, not a combo pile. Hapatra does not make -1/-1 counters at will — her first ability is a combat-damage trigger on an unevasive 2/2 — she monetises counters that *other* cards place, at a rate of one 1/1 deathtouch Snake per placement event. The 99 around her is built so that every counter becomes a body, every body becomes a card or a drain, and a narrow but genuine combo ceiling sits above a very strong grindy median.

how_it_wins:
The table sees a snake deck with a combo sheet stapled to it and treats you like a fuse. Here is what is actually true, and it is better news: Hapatra is a mint. Her combat trigger is a bonus on an unevasive 2/2 — never a plan. The half you build around is the payout: every time you put one or more -1/-1 counters on a creature, she hands you a 1/1 deathtouch Snake, one per placement event.

So stop hunting payoffs and start hunting sources. Of the eight sacrifice outlets here that cost no mana, exactly one — Yawgmoth, Thran Physician — also places a counter, and Devoted Druid only becomes a repeatable source with Mikaeus out to reset it. You draw a tutor in 78.0% of games: point the first one at a repeatable counter source, not at a drain. Blowfly Infestation, Serrated Arrows, Contagion Clasp and Black Sun's Zenith are the same job on different bodies — take whichever one your hand can cast this turn.

Most games you win by out-carding three people and then draining them, and that game assembles 67.2% of the time on a mean turn of 3.62. Clamp a Snake for two cards. Cash a spare body to Deadly Dispute or Village Rites at instant speed. Let Grim Haruspex collect your real creatures and Morbid Opportunist collect everyone else's. Every Snake you leave home also blanks an attacker of any size, so the board that draws you cards is the board nobody wants to swing into.

The ceiling is narrower than the sheet claims and you will cash it more often for knowing that. The kill is one repeatable source plus one converter that hits all three seats — Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance, or best of all Obelisk Spider, which drains on counter placement instead of on death and so runs roughly four times faster on a loop. You have a converter in hand in 51.9% of games, so when the second half arrives, pivot: deploy the source, count the table's spent interaction, and go. Blood Artist drains one player at a time — take the value, do not mistake him for a clock.
mana_base:
Twenty-nine black sources, twenty-nine green, against a hypergeometric target of twenty-two apiece. That is not comfortable, it is a surplus of seven on each side — and it comes out of thirty-six lands across twenty-four distinct entries, of which exactly zero enter tapped.

Twenty-two of those thirty-six make both colours; the other fourteen are basics. That is why lands alone put both pips at 96.2% on curve. The 90% yardstick is usually the thing ramp exists to rescue, and here it is cleared before a single rock is counted.

Now the disagreement the audit exists to find. Black carries 71.4% of the pip load — 40.0 pips spread over 34 cards, running as deep as triple-black — while holding a 50% source share; green carries 28.6% of the load, 16.0 pips over 15 cards, on the same 50%. Normally a gap that size costs something. It costs nothing here, because when 22 of your lands answer to either question, there is no split to get wrong.

Sixteen nonland producers finish the job: nine rocks, five dorks, two rituals, lifting on-curve to 98.8% black and 99.1% green and tilting the nonland source count green, 10 to 8, since dorks are Forests that block. Five of the rocks — Sol Ring, Mana Vault, Grim Monolith, Ashnod's Altar and Chrome Mox — score zero coloured sources under the audit's unconditional-mana rule. They are buying tempo, not fixing, and it shows in the shape of a game: mean available mana reaches 6.15 by turn six while the land-drop hit rate has already slid from 90.2% on turn three to 54.0%.

Nothing is free. City of Brass, Mana Confluence and Tarnished Citadel bill you in life, and Forbidden Orchard hands an opponent a Spirit every time you tap it. Restricted mana: none — not one source arrives with a spend-this-only-on clause attached. Zero tapped lands is an invoice written on a life total, and this list is built to pay it.
matchups:
Sweeper control believes you fold to a wrath. Wrong deck. Bitterblossom rebuilds every upkeep for a life, Skullclamp turns each dying 1/1 into two cards, Grim Haruspex collects your nontokens, and Blood Artist makes their sweeper a drain you get to aim.

So deploy in waves and lead with the half you do not mind losing. Tokens and cheap counter sources first, the enabler in hand until the pivot. Assume the wrath — across four players it is near-certain — and when it lands, recast Hapatra for two and carry on.

Pick your own sweeper on purpose. Black Sun's Zenith puts counters on each creature: a Snake per placement, food for Nest of Scarabs, and every opposing creature that dies with a counter handed to Necroskitter. Toxic Deluge places no counters and triggers none of that — save it for the turn you need the board gone and the life is genuinely spare.

Against stax and tax, believe the bad news quickly and then stop mourning it. There is no artifact removal, no enchantment removal and no counterspell here, so the lock does not come off. Race it or politick it (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial); do not burn three turns hunting an answer you did not pack.

Race with the half a tax cannot touch. Yawgmoth costs a life and a body and no mana, Bitterblossom triggers free on your upkeep, and Hapatra costs two and hits the table on turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 runs. Get under the second and third lock pieces, then keep activating while everyone else recounts their lands.

Politick with the truth, because it is the cheapest resource at the table. Say out loud that you are the seat with no answer to the Winter Orb, and ask the player holding the Krosan Grip to spend it. Keep the deal small, specific and expiring — one turn of your counters pointed elsewhere for one piece of enchantment removal.

Aggro believes a board of 1/1s is free damage. It is a wall of deathtouch that blanks their attacks regardless of size, and one board answering three players' attack plans is advantage no removal count will ever show you (strategy:card-advantage.virtual). Keep the Snakes home and stop swinging Hapatra into open blockers for a marginal trigger.

Spend life here on purpose rather than by accident. Yawgmoth, Phyrexian Reclamation, Bitterblossom, Toxic Deluge, City of Brass, Mana Confluence and Tarnished Citadel all bill the same total your engine runs on. Pick the one opponent whose clock is actually real and defend against that one, not the table (strategy:multiplayer.pod-management).

Combo decks believe you are a slow token deck worth ignoring, and here you should agree with them and cash it. Do not try to interact — nothing in this list touches an artifact or an enchantment. Rank combo proximity above every board threat, re-rank it each turn, and spend Grim Affliction, Fume Spitter, Serrated Arrows and Walking Ballista on a creature-based combo the moment they are live rather than holding them into the kill (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy).

Be honest about your own clock while you do it. A drain converter arrives on mean turn 3.34; the Blowfly line arrives on mean turn 4.10 in 16.3% of games and is not verified. You do not out-race a dedicated combo deck on assembly, so win the deflection instead: be the board nobody points interaction at, and go while three players watch each other (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection).

Creature midrange is the seat this deck was built for, and you beat them on two axes at once — their removal is poor against tokens and their attacks are poor into deathtouch. Hold your single-target removal until something is pointed at you; every one-for-one you cast on sight profits two bystanders for free (strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry).

Land Crumbling Ashes early in this matchup and let it grind. It destroys a creature carrying a -1/-1 counter at each of your upkeeps, from a permanent class fair creature decks mostly cannot answer. Seed it with Fume Spitter or Grim Affliction, and collect a Snake off every placement it makes.

Then win the long game with cards rather than combat. Skullclamp, Grim Haruspex, Morbid Opportunist, Deadly Dispute and Village Rites turn a stream of 1/1s into a stream of cards, and four-player games run long enough that a scaling engine is the default winning plan (strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock).

Graveyard hate is a smaller problem than it looks, so do not let it slow you down. A Rest in Peace effect costs you Necroskitter, Phyrexian Reclamation and Eternal Witness and costs you nothing else — Snakes, counters and drains never touch a graveyard. Keep playing the value game at full speed and let the seat that spent a card on you feel good about it.
mulligan:
Everyone keeps the hand with Nest of Scarabs and Blood Artist in it. Do not be everyone. Those cards are exchange rates, and an exchange rate with nothing to exchange is a blank. The keep test is one question: does this hand reach a repeatable -1/-1 source?

You can afford to be strict, because the deck is forgiving. You keep the first seven 79.9% of the time and average 0.243 mulligans; Hapatra hits the table on turn two in 9,970 of 10,000 runs. A keep does not have to contain the engine — it has to cast the commander on schedule and find one.

Keep on sight: two to four lands with Hapatra castable on two, plus any of Yawgmoth, Devoted Druid, Blowfly Infestation or a tutor. Keep the two-lander that has Birds of Paradise, Llanowar Elves, Elvish Mystic, Sol Ring, Lotus Petal or Dark Ritual attached — that hand casts the commander a turn early with a play left over. Keep Skullclamp with any token maker, and keep Bitterblossom alone, because it is a body every turn and it rebuilds through a wrath by itself.

Ship the five-lander with no tutor and no dork. You have seen the curve: four zero-drops, sixteen ones, nineteen twos, and two cards above four mana. That hand is holding two cards it will never spend. Ship converters with no source — Blood Artist, Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance are the classic trap keep. Ship hands built on Mikaeus alone; he is your only six-drop, he places no counters, and he needs a specific partner to do anything at all. Ship one-landers even with a mox, because a mox that finds no second land loses your commander.

Treat Scurry Oak, Ivy Lane Denizen and Host of the Hereafter as bodies rather than as routes — the lines they are famous for are unsettled here, and you do not mulligan toward something this manual will not assert. On the way to six, compress to two things: black mana on turn two, and one card that either places counters repeatedly or fetches one that does.
threat_assessment:
The table looks at a 2/2 legend and a couple of 1/1 tokens and files you under snake deck. Let them. That read is the most valuable thing you own, and it costs you nothing until you spend it.

Bank the turns it buys. Hapatra lands on turn 2 in 9,970 of 10,000 goldfish runs, so stop deliberating over turn 2 and spend that thinking on turn 3. A payoff joins her by mean turn 3.6 in 67.2% of games — play the first four turns as a value deck, because that is exactly what they are.

The second thing the table believes is the dangerous one, and it may have come from you. The combo sheet claims nineteen two-card infinites; stack 001 verifies one — Mikaeus alongside Devoted Druid — and refutes six. Never sell the nineteen in a Rule 0 conversation — say bracket 4, say eleven Game Changers, say one verified line, and let the honesty buy you a seat the number would have cost you.

Play the eleven unresolved lines the way you talk about them. Unresolved is not false; it means you do not tap out for one. Cast Blowfly Infestation, Scurry Oak and Host of the Hereafter as counter sources and boards, take the value, and if a loop appears take it with a spare body and a land still up.

The Hapatra-and-Blowfly hand arrives in 16.3% of games and 12.5% by turn 6. Accept it as a bonus and steer nothing toward it — no mulligan, no tutor, no turn built on its arrival.

Three permanents flip you from ignored to archenemy, and Hapatra is none of them.

Yawgmoth is the first. He is the only free repeatable counter source in the deck, which means the table's removal finds him the turn he resolves. Put him down with a second body already on the board and a turn that converts — anything less spends your scarcest card for nothing.

Mikaeus is the second, and he announces himself. Six mana against a mean 6.15 available on turn 6 means you tap low to cast the card everyone reads as the combo piece. Those two are the verified pairings in stack 001, so cast him with Devoted Druid or Walking Ballista already down; otherwise hold him and cast two things instead.

The third is quiet and it is the one that actually kills. A converter that hits every seat — Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance, Obelisk Spider — landing beside a repeatable source is your pivot trigger. You hold a converter in 51.9% of games and 41.5% by turn 6, so keep it in hand for that turn instead of deploying it early to be shot.

Sequence to keep the cover on. Lead with the token half — Bitterblossom, Snakes, cheap counter sources — because it reads defensive and rebuilds through a wrath by itself. Hold the enabler. Deploy fast mana on the turn it buys a threat, not on turn one for the look of it.

Know exactly what spends the cover: eleven Game Changers. Chrome Mox, Mox Diamond, Mana Vault, Grim Monolith, Demonic Tutor, Vampiric Tutor, Imperial Seal, Worldly Tutor, Survival of the Fittest, Orcish Bowmasters, The One Ring. The turn one of those resolves your Snakes stop reading as chump blockers, so fire tutors on a turn when a louder seat has just done something (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection).

You draw a tutor in 78.0% of games and 67.6% by turn 6. Point the first one at a repeatable counter source, never at a converter — the converters find you on their own.

The One Ring is the loudest card in this list. Cast it for the cards, on a turn you can afford the life and the attention, and never as a protection turn you are hoping nobody prices.

When you take the archenemy seat, take it once and take it counted. Count open mana at every seat first, and assume every held answer appears the moment you present the loop (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window). Prefer the attempt that leaves Bitterblossom, a converter and a board of Snakes behind if it fails.

A thin record is an advantage the moment you play to it. Three opponents are holding up mana against nineteen kills you do not have, and that discount applies to every value turn you take in the meantime. Pace for the median, hold the ceiling as opportunism (strategy:critical-mass), and move when the count says move — this deck wins far more games by out-drawing the table than by ever finding a loop.
upgrades:
Eleven thousand seven hundred and ninety-nine cards were eligible and ten got through. There is no bench behind this list, so every name below is a pool scout — a first read over the whole legal green-black pool, not a shuffle of cards already in the box.

Four of those ten aim at one number, which tells you how lopsided that number is. Interaction here covers one of the five permanent classes. Beast Within sits at EDHREC rank 25 and Scavenging Ooze at 1,570, and together they move that one to five; Nature's Claim comes in at one mana against the corpus's three-mana ceiling for interaction, and Assassin's Trophy at rank 124 is the flexible middle. Spending 40% of a ten on a single axis is unusual. A one-out-of-five is unusual.

The second cluster is a redundancy figure. Mikaeus plus a free sacrifice outlet assembles 9.5% of the time on its own, 50.4% with a tutor helping — the widest gap on the board, and the signature of a component that is one card deep. Gravecrawler at rank 687, Reassembling Skeleton at 767 and Forsaken Miner at 2,465 all route around it, each returning from the graveyard as a nontoken body the sacrifice outlets can actually keep eating.

The funding comes from the ramp column, which sits four copies over its 10-to-12 target — so four of the ten cuts come from there rather than from anything doing engine work. And the bracket line does not move: 4 before, 4 after, on all ten. These are extensions, not escalations.

Two honest notes on the arithmetic. Every combo line a scout opens is stamped needs a stack scenario, which in this deck is not a formality — one census verified a loop and refuted six pairings that read just as well on paper. And the thinnest component of all, Blowfly Infestation at 16.3% assembled, returned nothing: no pool card shares its role signature, no combo line pairs it with anything already sleeved. The search came back empty, and that is worth knowing before the ten below start looking comprehensive.

The famous misses lose on arithmetic too. The Great Henge ranks 235 and prices off greatest power, which on a board of 1/1 Snakes leaves it near nine mana. Peer into the Abyss costs seven in a deck whose modal cost is two. Triskelion wants a partner for a line Walking Ballista already runs.
